taxonomy.subtopic: Retrograde blood supply and proximal-pole avascular necrosis

questions.stem_html:
A 24-year-old cyclist falls onto an outstretched hand. He has focal tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox, but initial radiographs show no fracture. The wrist is immobilized. Repeat imaging 12 days later shows a nondisplaced fracture through the waist of the scaphoid. A diagram highlights arterial entry along the distal portion of the bone.

Which complication is the proximal fragment at greatest risk of developing?

options.text_html: Osteomyelitis from hematogenous seeding of the distal fragment
Median nerve transection within the carpal tunnel
Volkmann ischemic contracture from brachial artery occlusion
Avascular necrosis due to interruption of retrograde intraosseous blood flow
Radial head subluxation from annular ligament rupture

questions.explanation_html: Most scaphoid perfusion enters distally and travels proximally. A waist fracture can isolate the proximal pole from its retrograde arterial supply. Disruption of distal arterial inflow can leave the proximal pole ischemic, leading to avascular necrosis and nonunion.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: A closed fracture without bacteremia does not preferentially cause distal-fragment osteomyelitis.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Scaphoid fracture can cause pain and nonunion but does not typically transect the median nerve.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Volkmann contracture follows severe forearm ischemia, usually after supracondylar injury or compartment syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Radial head subluxation is an elbow injury and is unrelated to the scaphoid blood supply.

questions.educational_objective: Use the scaphoid's retrograde vascular anatomy to predict proximal-pole avascular necrosis after a waist fracture, even when initial radiographs are normal.
